items.excerpt: 会期：2026/07/11～2026/07/12 会場：三重県文化会館 小ホール［三重県］ 公式サイト：https://hatetocheek.com/kimitomo2026/ 「しんどいのはみんな同じ」という言葉が「共感」「慰め」の形を借りて発せられるとき、なぜ、何が問題なのか。社会構造や規範、他者からの一方的なジャッジがもたらす抑圧の経験が「それぞれ異なる」という差異自体が覆い隠され、「ないこと」にされてしまうからだ。とりわけこの言葉がマジョリティからマイノリティに向けて発せられるとき、互いに「ともだち」と思っている関係には、わかりあえなさの深い断絶が口を開ける。だが、マジョリティ／マイノリティの構造自体も絶対的で固定的なものではなく、状況によって流動的に揺らぎ、勾配が変動し、あるいは多層的に重なり合っている。「喫煙なんて、将来の赤ちゃんのために良くない」という「善意の心配」がはらむ、「女性は当然、出産するべき」というジェンダー規範。社会に空気のように浸透し、洗い流そうとしてもこびりついたシスヘテロ規範や無意識の偏見に基づくマイクロアグレッション、「言い方が大げさだ」と非難の矛先
items.body: 会期：2026/07/11～2026/07/12 会場：三重県文化会館 小ホール［三重県］ 公式サイト：https://hatetocheek.com/kimitomo2026/ 「しんどいのはみんな同じ」という言葉が「共感」「慰め」の形を借りて発せられるとき、なぜ、何が問題なのか。社会構造や規範、他者からの一方的なジャッジがもたらす抑圧の経験が「それぞれ異なる」という差異自体が覆い隠され、「ないこと」にされてしまうからだ。とりわけこの言葉がマジョリティからマイノリティに向けて発せられるとき、互いに「ともだち」と思っている関係には、わかりあえなさの深い断絶が口を開ける。だが、マジョリティ／マイノリティの構造自体も絶対的で固定的なものではなく、状況によって流動的に揺らぎ、勾配が変動し、あるいは多層的に重なり合っている。「喫煙なんて、将来の赤ちゃんのために良くない」という「善意の心配」がはらむ、「女性は当然、出産するべき」というジェンダー規範。社会に空気のように浸透し、洗い流そうとしてもこびりついたシスヘテロ規範や無意識の偏見に基づくマイクロアグレッション、「言い方が大げさだ」と非難の矛先を巧妙にすり替えるトーンポリシング、そしてセクシュアル・マイノリティが日常の端々で直面する困難を、本作はテンポのよい会話劇で解像度を上げてあぶり出していく。2025年の初演後、東京と三重で再演された。 ［撮影：水澤桃花］ 舞台は、地下にある寂れたカラオケ店。上手に受付カウンター、中央にカラオケルーム、下手に公衆電話ボックスのような一人用の喫煙ブースが設置されている。階段を降りながら、ナンパ目的でしつこく声をかけてくる男に罵声を浴びせるノンバイナリーの野澤。高校の同級生・由海の結婚式の途中、野澤のパートナーのノリちゃんが気分が悪くなり、付き添いとして途中退出したため、カラオケ店で飲み直すことにしたという。そこに、幼馴染の園（その）と、園の恋人で同じ会社の先輩でもある甲斐田が合流する。カラオケ店は、野澤と園の大学時代の友人・衛の親が経営し、衛はアルバイトをしながら音楽活動を続けている。 ［撮影：水澤桃花］ 久しぶりに会った野澤、園、衛の3人と、野澤と衛とは初対面の甲斐田。アルコールの力も借りた空元気と気まずさが同居する二次会は、近況報告の会話のなかに、トランスジェンダー女性であるノリちゃんが直面するさまざまな困難を浮かび上がらせていく。ノリちゃんが結婚式で吐いてしまったのは、新婦の由海が「すべての恋人に幸せを」と言って野澤たちにブーケを手渡したからだ。「色んな愛の形がある」とスピーチしてブーケトスした由海は、園の目には感動的に映るが、「多様な性を認めて祝福しよう」という由海の言動は、自らが異性愛というマジョリティ側にいるという自覚に欠けており、善意で発せられたものであるからこそ野澤とノリちゃんを傷つけてしまう。 だが、もともと体調が良くなかったノリちゃんが吐いてしまった理由は、ブーケトスだけではなかった。前の職場では、「ありのままの姿を応援します！」というコピーとともに自社広告に載せられ、ダイバーシティ推進の広告塔にされかけていた。そして、LGBTQフレンドリーを掲げる（ただしHPに掲載されているのはほぼゲイの経験談である）転職先の会社に希望を見出すも、採用担当者から「女子トイレは使わないで」と真っ先に言われ、そのことをSNSに投稿したら炎上してしまい、リストカットを繰り返す精神的に不安定な状態に追い込まれていた。 ノリちゃんが不在の場で、さらに野澤を追い詰めるのが、甲斐田からの「相談」だ。なんと、ノリちゃんの転職先は園と甲斐田の会社であり、甲斐田はノリちゃんの上司候補だと明かされる。「どう対応したらよいか」とアドバイスを求める甲斐田は一見誠実だが、彼自身、トランス女性とトランス男性の違いもわからず、基礎的な知識すらない。野澤は混乱してうろたえながらも、「でもめちゃくちゃ特別な人間てわけじゃないんですよ」「一人一人違うので、どこまで許容できるかみたいなことが」「ノリちゃんは、やっぱり男性としては扱ってほしくない、というか、だからあの、それだけだとは思うんですよ、基本的には」と説明する。だが、「俺らは良いんだけど、社員の、まあ女性が」と言う甲斐田の周囲には、トランスフォビアがまとわりついている。 ［撮影：水澤桃花］ 園もまた、ノリちゃんのことを快く思っておらず、「佐川さん」とよそよそしく苗字で呼び、それを察している野澤も園にはノリちゃんを会わせていない。トランス女性に対して園が抱く嫌悪感は、もう一人の高校時代の友人、まーちゃんについてのエピソードで示される。美大に進んだまーちゃんは、アート界の不均衡なジェンダーバランスや（おそらくそれに基づく）性被害に遭い、SNSでトランス女性排除に回ってしまった。だが、園は「あんだけ男からクソみたいな目にあったら、男の体で？ みたいな、受け入れられないのもわかるけどね」と発言する。園も元彼から暴力を振るわれた経験がある。だが園には、トランス女性が日常的に直面する偏見や困難に加えて、（トランスフォビアと女性蔑視という二重の負荷によって）トランス女性も・性的嫌がらせの対象になりうる事態がまったく見えていない。 価値観の齟齬や深い断絶は、園と甲斐田という異性愛のカップルの間にも存在する。「結婚しても子どもは欲しくない」と言う園に対し、「結婚したら当然子どもをもつべき」「子どものいる家庭＝幸せ」という価値観に何の疑問ももたない甲斐田との仲は、ギクシャクときしみ始める。また、本作は、男性どうしの格差やマイクロアグレッション、男性社会の抑圧もすくい上げて描写する。甲斐田と衛の間には正社員／アルバイトという格差があり、「音楽で成功できず、パラサイトシングルで、甲斐田のように結婚して子どもをもつ未来図など描けない」というコンプレックスを衛は抱えている。だが、男性性の規範を体現したような甲斐田自身、親兄弟や会社に染みついたホモソーシャルな空気に否応なく飲み込まれていることに、恐怖と息苦しさを感じていることが吐露される。 それぞれの人間関係の軋轢や抑圧が増幅され、蓄積されて臨界点を迎え、衛が甲斐田に水をぶっかけるという突発的な暴力の形で噴き出す。園は「野澤も佐川さんも大変だと思うけど、でも大変なのは皆同じじゃん」と諌めるが、野澤は「あたしとあんたのしんどさは、違うんじゃない？」と指摘する。採用担当者との相談の日、ノリちゃんはトイレのことを言われても、泣いたり怒ったりせず、「普通」に見えたと甲斐田は言う。だが、「その“普通”でいるために、あの日ノリちゃんがどれだけ努力したかっていうのは、分かりますか？」と野澤は尋ねる。「人間なんです、あたしも、だから一生懸命、どうしたらここで受け入れてもらえるかってずっと考えてるんですよ」と。「その、頑張ってきた全部、を、皆同じとか、しんどいとか、そんな、そんな言葉で、あんたがナシにしないで、お願い」──野澤の言葉は、園が「ともだち」と思っているからこそ深く突き刺さる。そして、「……よかったよ、あんたがそっち側で」「そっちは眺める側だから、見なくて済んでよかったよ」と園に向けられる痛烈な皮肉は、「演劇の舞台」という構造とも重ねられ、「マイノリティの物語を安全な距離から一方的に眺め、消費する観客」に対しても向けられるものだろう。 「もうやめよう。おしまいにしよう」という野澤の台詞は、「噛み合わず、徒労に終わるだけの会話はもうやめよう」という文字通りの意味の裏に、「園との友人関係の破綻」を示唆する。それぞれ野澤と園を演じる升味加耀と川村瑞樹が共同主宰するユニット「果てとチーク」の名前は、「hate to hope」に由来し、この2つの単語を英語で読むと「ヘイト」と「希望」という正反対の意味が浮かび上がる。「果てとほっぺ（頬）」というローマ字読みと、「ヘイトと希望」という英単語の二重の意味を、異なる角度から同時に読むことは可能か。「ヘイト」の只中に「希望」はどう見出せるのか。言葉遊びの駆使のなかに、切実な希求が込められている。 ［撮影：水澤桃花］ 後編では、こうしたダブルミーニングを念頭に置きつつ、野澤と園をめぐる終盤の展開を見ていく。ここには、「傷を再び反復しない形でどうやって語ることができるのか」というマイノリティが抱えるジレンマと根本的な問題が横たわっている。また、「劇中、なぜノリちゃんは不在化されているのか」という問いに焦点を当てるとともに、「カラオケボックス」という設定の秀逸さと、「個室の喫煙ブース」という装置の両義性についても掘り下げる。 鑑賞日：2026/07/11（土） （後編へ）※9/11公開予定

items.excerpt: 横浜・Art Center NEWにて、日本全国のオルタナティブスペースが集結するアートフェア「NEW PLATFORMーAlternative JAPANー」が開催されます。 オルタナティブスペースとは、美術館やコマーシャルギャラリーとは異なる独自の方法で表現活動を続けるアートスペースを指します。「NEW PLATFORM」では、そうしたオルタナティブスペースが一堂に集い、その実践や運営について共有する場を目指して、年に一度行なわれています。 今年度は北海道から沖縄までの13の都道府県より、23のスペースが参加。各地域の実践から日本のアートシーンを捉え直し、新たな活動の可能性を再考するとともに、各地のアートスペース同士をつなぐ交流の場を創出します。 さらに、アジアにルーツを持つ作家を対象に公募を行なったアーティスト・イン・レジデンス・プログラム「NEW AIR 2026」の成果発表展も同時に開催されます。 開催イベント ■出展者同士によるクロストーク 日時｜2026/09/11（金）17:30〜19:00 [衣食住とアート]:コミュニティ、飲食、日常の中での実践 日時｜2026/09

items.body: For a few years, I have had this funny vision of Antwerp’s Summer Bummer festival taking place on a beach near a body of water. I had sunshine, seagull calls and good vibes in this fantasy. In reality, the venue, a rock club called Trix, is located on a busy road amongst high-rise apartment buildings just outside of downtown Antwerp. So, no seagulls, no beach and even the sun was being fickle. It troubled me, what could be the source for this misconception? The only part I had right was the ‘good vibes’. From the moment the first band started up in the darkened main hall on Friday afternoon to the closing tones of a bass-clarinet and electronics show on the intimate cafe stage late Saturday night, there was always something to hear, records to dig, people to talk shop with, and art to make — hardly leaving time to lament the waning days of the summer. Within the compact time-frame, starting late afternoon and ending around midnight on Friday and Saturday, festival organizers Koen Vandenhout and Christel Kumpen ran a tight program. Concerts were lined-up one after the other with a short break built-in to give the 200+ audience a chance to eat some dinner without developing FOMO. Plus, the sets ping-ponged from the main hall side to the cafe side, so there was always a chance to hit the bar if desired. Between the two halls, merch tables were arranged on all sides, making it dangerous to the wallet to traverse the venue. Parent organization of the festival Sound in Motion’s own Dropa-Disc label was present, as well as a record dealer with a selection of rare taste and local radio station Radio Centraal. If one purchased a t-shirt, or happened to have an extra one on hand, he or she (more likely than not: he) could head into the screen printing workshop and make their own with a festival design. Additionally, set in an adjacent room, musicians Cath Roberts and Tullis Rennie invited festival goers to record and manipulate sounds in a laboratory of their own design. When the weather was cooperative, one could visit the courtyard to procure some homemade food. Alexander von Schlippenbach and Paal Nilssen-Love The Sound In Motion website has the tagline, “Adventurous Music and Things”, and since we have got the things part out of the way, let us talk adventurous music . Not just a free-jazz festival, Summer Bummer’s scope this year included several avant-noise and electronics acts along with some of the most exciting musicians working (primarily) in Europe today. There was something for everyone, for example the ear-bleedingly loud Integral , a quartet comprised of Julien Desprez (guitar), Claire Gapenne (electronics and vocals), Christine Abelnour (sax) and Lukas Koenig (drums) that went from beguiling to battering, to the opening act, Kabas Sun Dogs, a Belgian band who had invited Canadian saxophonist Karen Ng and guitarist Jonathan Horne for a slowly unfolding exploration of both understatement and spirited groove. Rodrigo Amado, Joelle Leandre and Gerald Cleaver Highlights festooned the program, including a first time duo of drummer Paal Nilssen-Love and the legendary pianist Alexander von Schlippenbach as well as new trio formed by Rodrigo Amado with bassist Joelle Leandre and drummer Gerald Cleaver . In the duo’s extended set, Schlippenbach performed a chain of melodic ideas and Thelonius Monk song snippets that Nilssen-Love challenged with closely attuned force and precision. After a cautious opening, the trio of Amado, Leandre and Cleaver edged their way into the set, gathering momentum to the findcommon ground, letting Amado release his powerful tenor, Leandre impress with speed and expressiveness, and Cleaver move seamlessly between texture and forceful pulse. Daughter, Daughter The formidable quartet of Daughter, Daughter, comprised of Camila Nebbia and Amalie Dahl (saxophones), Elizabeth Coudoux (cello) and Sun Mi Hong (drums), performed a blend of composition and free-jazz improvisation showcasing both individual contributions as well as whole group interactions. The Berlin formation Das B , featuring Mazen Kerbaj (trumpet), Magda Mayas (piano), Tony Buck (drums) and Mike Majkowski (bass) was given the designation as a “super group“ in the program and their set did not refute this. Ostensibly deconstructing John Coltrane’s A Love Supreme , the quartet engaged in an exploratory and expansive sound collage complete with a trumpet played via surgical tubing and prepared piano that made the acoustic sound electric. Arguably one of the strongest shows of the festival. Das B Additionally, percussionist and singer Maria Portugal presented her EROSÃO Septet (Lotte Anker and Angelika Niescier on saxes , Matthias M üller and Moritz Wesp on trombones , Carl Ludwig H übsch on tuba and Reza Askari on bass ) , which performed a set of mid-tempo songs, both self-penned and from Brazilian composers, laced with some spicy improvisations. The next day, Portugal appeared in an exceptional duo with pianist Marta Warelis . As opposed to the septet, in which the music was a presented in more traditional structures, the songs themselves were de-composed and integrated organically with the ideas flowing from the pianist whose gentle and spacious playing grew progressively more ferocious. Marta Warelis and Maria Portugal Rounding out the program were two bass clarinet focused sets and several quite noisy ones. Representing the louder side, in addition to the aforementioned Integral, were New Best Friends (featuring Ng and Horne along with bassist Aaron Lumley and drummer Nasim L-P Navarro), the duo of Laurentiu Cotac and Diana Miron, and Mopcut with Desprez, Koenig and electronicist/vocalist Audrey Chen. Of these three, New Best Friends balanced their clamorous impulses best with a flowing set of improvisations. Bookending the festival were two bass clarinet sets. On the first day, John McCowen explored the extended tonalities of the acoustic contra-bass clarinet, exploiting the instrument’s multiphonic capabilities. Closing the festival, Hanna De Backer , in collaboration with the electronics of Yves De Mey , extended her instrument’s sonic possibilities to the outer realms. Overall, a musically adventurous and enjoyable festival, and although quite satisfied, I was still bothered by one thing: my imaginary festival on a beach. So, after some detective work, I believe I finally pinpointed the source of my whimsical misconception. In 2019, Rodrigo Amado's The Attic released the album Summer Bummer , recorded at the festival in 2018 and whose cover is an image of three cut-out figures sitting on a beach under a cloudless blue sky, looking out at the ocean. I didn’t know I was so impressionable! Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.album: ザ・メンジンジャーズ（The Menzingers）『Everything I Ever Saw』ガスライト・アンセムを彷彿させる歌メロが印象的な8thアルバム
items.tags: 洋楽 洋楽ポップ／ロック bounce 2026 September 洋楽 洋楽ポップ／ロック # パンク 洋楽 THE MENZINGERS
items.excerpt: 結成20周年を迎えたUSパンク4人組による8作目がリリース。音楽的にはガスライト・アンセムを彷彿させるブルージーな歌メロが印象的で、3分台とコンパクトにまとめられた楽曲も聴きやすい。アコギや鍵盤を用いたアレンジもそつがなく、地に足の着いた演奏から放たれるスケールの大きなメロディーが最高に気持ちいいのだ。繰り返し聴きたくなる滋味溢れる作品である。

items.album: ターシャ（Tasha）『You Are Spring!』ジャミーラ・ウッズらと歌声を重ね、生命が息吹く春の美しさを表現した4作目
items.tags: 洋楽 洋楽ポップ／ロック intoxicate 2026 August 洋楽 洋楽ポップ／ロック # インディー・フォーク 洋楽 TASHA GREGORY UHLMANN JAMILA WOODS L'RAIN
items.excerpt: シカゴからNYへ拠点を移したSSW、Tashaの4thアルバム。本作もギタリスト／プロデューサーのGregory Uhlmannとの共作です。R&BアーティストのJamila WoodsとL’Rainの歌声が心地よく重なる“Spring”から始まり、自身がクラリネットを演奏した“Special”、ペンシルベニア州の町の名からインスパイアされた“Clarion”など全11曲。冬から春へと季節が巡り、生命が息吹く春の美しさを鮮やかに表現した作品となっています。インディー〜フォークミュージックの表現の枠を越え、彼女の作る音楽の美しさを体感できる1枚です。

items.body:
BLACKPINK’s JISOO is stepping into character for her latest collaboration with London-based fashion house self-portrait.

Titled Portraits of a Screen Star, the fashion campaign casts JISOO in a series of imagined audition tapes, with the singer and actress taking on four distinct cinematic characters. Shot in Seoul by photographer Oliver Hadlee Pearch, each instalment is set to reveal a different side of her artistry and performance.

The series has premiered with The Enigma, which sees JISOO embodying a curious, whimsical and quietly amused character. For the first instalment, she wears a grey button knit playsuit, a red check frayed knit jacket, and a purple faux leather skirt.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by self-portrait (@mrselfportrait)

Speaking about the project, JISOO shared that the campaign gave her the opportunity to explore something new through each role.

“I was so excited to star in this new series of short films with Han and self-portrait. It allowed me to try something completely new and each character I played required something different from me,” she said.

JISOO added that each character’s wardrobe played an important part in shaping her performances.

“The evolution of the character's wardrobe was how I found the nuance in each performance,” she shared. “I have worn self-portrait for many years and the pieces make me feel like I can do anything — this time, they let me dream that I could be anyone.”

Three more characters, each with their own personality and visual identity, are set to be unveiled throughout September.

items.body:
Idris Elba is bringing his dance-music alter ego to Bangkok.

Performing as IDRIS, the actor, DJ, and producer will take over Cloud 11 Theatre on 26 September for a one-night-only show presented by Collective Minds. The night will also mark the arrival of his record label and music platform, Sound International, in the Thai capital.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Sound International (@sound.intl)

Before becoming internationally known for his acting career, Elba had already found his footing behind the decks. Introduced to DJing by his uncle, who ran a London sound system, he later balanced acting with DJ sets at club night Twice as Nice.

His career as IDRIS has since taken him to Ibiza institutions including Pacha, Pikes, and Hï, as well as festival stages at Glastonbury and Coachella. Behind the decks, he brings together the Afro, calypso, and reggae sounds he grew up with alongside tech-house and progressive rhythms.

Sound International continues that musical lineage. Elba created the label in tribute to his uncle's original sound system, building a home for the global house sound that has shaped his DJ career.

Joining IDRIS at Cloud 11 Theatre are Wildealer and Elaheh, rounding out the lineup for the Bangkok show. Click here to purchase tickets.

items.body:
Singapore ENGENEs, get ready to step into ENHYPEN’s world.

The K-pop group’s ENHYPEN VR CONCERT : DESTINY, happening from 18 September to 4 October, is headed to Golden Village Bugis+, offering fans an immersive concert experience that combines music, cinematic storytelling, and VR technology.

Following ENHYPEN’s previous VR experience, DESTINY brings the group’s signature vampire universe into a new dimension. Equipped with VR headsets provided at the venue, fans will find themselves inside the story and experience the members from an up-close perspective.

The VR concert will feature performances of 'Knife', 'Big Girls Don’t Cry', and 'CRIMINAL LOVE', weaving the tracks into a story centred on pursuit, connection, and fate.

Each ticket will also come with exclusive collectibles, available while stocks last. Fans attending from 18 to 26 September will receive a random DESTINY photo card from six designs, a DESTINY sticker, and an exclusive A5 postcard. From 27 September to 4 October, attendees will receive a random DESTINY photo card, a DESTINY photocard sleeve, and an exclusive A5 postcard.

Tickets go on sale on 9 September at 3 PM via Golden Village's website, mobile app, and box offices.

Check out the ticket prices below:

Student: S$35

GVMC: S$38

Public: S$40

For the first time, Golden Village is also introducing a student price for its VR concerts. Students can purchase tickets at S$35 for sessions before 6 PM from Mondays to Fridays, excluding the eve of and Public Holidays. A valid student pass must be presented at the Golden Village Bugis+ Box Office.

The Singapore run follows launches of ENHYPEN VR CONCERT : DESTINY in South Korea and other international markets.

items.body:
Japanese singer-songwriter Mahiru is heading to Singapore for her first-ever concert in the country.

The singer will bring Mahiru ONE-MAN ASIA TOUR 2026-2027 Auralisia in Singapore to Victoria Theatre on 29 November, with the show set to begin at 8 PM. The Singapore stop follows performances in Taipei and Hong Kong.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Live Nation SG (@livenationsg)

Auralisia is a coined term combining “Aura,” “Lyric,” and 'Florisia', the title of the tour's theme song. Built around the idea of “the fragrance of a special flower,” the tour aims to create a distinct set of memories — or “fragrance” — in each city.

“It’d be great if we can create a different fragrance in Singapore from those of Taipei and Hong Kong,” Mahiru shared in a statement. “To those whom I will be meeting for the first time, and those who have supported me along the way — I’m looking forward to seeing all of you that day.”

Mahiru made her major-label debut with Warner Music Japan in January. She has since topped KKBOX's Japanese New Songs Daily Chart in Taiwan and Hong Kong, while tickets to her solo concert at Zepp New Taipei sold out within 30 minutes.

Mastercard cardholders will have access to a presale beginning 17 September at 10 AM, ahead of the general sale on 18 September at 10 AM via Ticketmaster Singapore. This concert is presented by Live Nation Singapore.

items.body:
VERIVERY are back with their eighth mini album, CONFETTI.

Released on 7 September, the five-track EP arrives almost a year after the group’s single album Lost and Found. This time around, DONGHEON, GYEHYEON, YEONHO, YONGSEUNG, and KANGMIN embrace a more playful and relaxed side of VERIVERY, finding joy in the everyday moments that can become highlights of their own.

Inspired by the image of confetti bursting over the brightest moments of a festival, CONFETTI sees the group turning small pieces of everyday happiness into music.

“I hope this album can be a small source of happiness in your daily life,” GYEHYEON shared.

The record opens with 'Way to Zero', an electronic dance-pop number about trusting your instincts instead of searching for the perfect answer. It leads into title track 'Don’t Panic!', a bright funk-pop song encouraging listeners to enjoy the present amid the repetition of everyday life.

Also featured on the EP is 'DRAMA', a disco-pop fan song whose lyrics were written by all five members as they look towards continuing their story with VERRER.

CONFETTI also marks VERIVERY’s first unit activities. YONGSEUNG and KANGMIN team up as the Y2K unit for speed garage track 'Touch', while DONGHEON, YEONHO, and GYEHYEON form the DYG unit for the full-band-driven 'Eye Contact (눈 마주쳤지)'.

“This is an album we were more involved in creating than ever before, so we hope you’ll listen closely to the message VERIVERY wanted to share!” YONGSEUNG said.

Following the release of CONFETTI, the group are set to embark on their GIVE ME FIVE, KEEP THAT VIBE tour. The run kicks off in Seoul on 3 October before continuing across 10 additional stops in Asia and Europe.

items.body:
EVAN is carving out his identity as a self-producing solo artist with his first mini-album. Released on 7 September, DEATH OF ME sees the K-pop soloist taking the creative lead across all eight tracks, spanning songwriting, production, and the record's overall creative direction.

Ahead of its arrival, DEATH OF ME surpassed 500,000 Spotify pre-saves, making it the most pre-saved album by a K-pop soloist in the platform's history, according to BELIFT LAB.

At the centre of the record is 'Death of Me', a heavy pop R&B title track co-written by EVAN. The song captures his determination to stay true to himself as he steps into a new chapter, anchored by the declaration: “Ain’t the death of me.”

Its accompanying music video puts EVAN onstage and revolves around the concept of “LIVE”, playing with the word's dual meaning of being alive and performing.

Across the rest of DEATH OF ME, EVAN moves between pop, alternative rock, indie pop, dream pop, and R&B. The eight-track project opens with 'Not Enough', 'Noise', and 'Ride or Die', before moving into 'Twilight', 'Immature', 'Overflow', and closing track 'Going Home'.

Through the record, EVAN charts a progression from intensity towards introspection, further establishing the musical direction he wants to pursue as a solo artist.

Hopeful Melodies Pair With Grief & Anxiety-Inspired Lyrics On Lotus Flower's 'A Night of the Jumps'

8 September 2026

When he chose the moniker 'Lotus Flower' for himself, it was clear Shriraj Sagara wasn't trying to hide that he is influenced by Radiohead, his voice often choosing the relaxed, high-pitched falsetto singing that has defined frontman Thom Yorke's work. The Ahmedabad-rooted, Berlin-based musician continues to gradually build upon that influence in his latest EP 'A Night of the Jumps'.

The melodies of the falsetto singing lend more to the atmosphere of synth arpeggios, horn lines and steady percussion rather than inviting the limelight. Meanwhile, Shriraj's compositions carry a more uplifting quality even as they deal with an unsettled mixture of anxiety, grief and vulnerability. Notably, the pounding rhythm section of opener 'Ceremony', unlike the formerly mentioned namesake influence, keeps things more communal and inviting than introspective, even as the song attempts to capture the coldness and disorientation of a difficult winter.

The subtly gritty and detuned synth foundations of 'A Small Town Cries' harken more to the nostalgia found in works by acts like Boards of Canada, though the lyrics draw from fragments of news from Israel's war on Gaza. The track Shriraj join hands again with his brother Shantanu Sagara for another DIY music video, though with less production value than their previous stellar work 'Wilting'.

Check out 'A Night of the Jumps' below and follow Shriraj Sagara on Instagram for more information.

items.body: Laurie Osborne (Appleblim) describes Liminal Tides with a series of antinomies: awake / asleep, self / no self, and conscious / unconscious mind / no-mind. To these, one could add Bristol / Berlin. It’s no secret that Osborne has spent much of his career as Appleblim between these two cities. While he picked up the mantle Appleblim in London, DJing early dubstep at the foundational FWD>> clubnights, he began producing the stuff upon moving to Bristol in 2006. Bristol is also where his two record labels got their start: Skull Disco (2005-2008) which he ran with Sam Shackelton, and the solo imprint Apple Pips (2008-present, though largely inactive since 2013). At the same time Appleblim got big in Berlin, Ricardo Villalobos and the rest of the minimal techno crowd taking to the unique strain of dubstep pushed by Skull Disco. And soon after Brexit, Appleblim relocated to Berlin, where he teaches synthesis at Catalyst and composes music, both at home ‘in the box’ and at a Funkhaus studiospace shared between friends. Even still, Osborne retains links to Bristol, for instance, as one half of the acclaimed Wrecked Lightship project with Bristolian Adam Winchester. All this to say that Liminal Tides sounds like an oceanic midway point between Bristol and Berlin. The album is filled with all gaseous drums and translucent tides of texture, a triple-point between the more hauntological side of post-post-dubstep (artists like fellow Bristol-to-Berlin producer and Sneaker Social Club signee Low End Activist come to mind) that channels the 1990s doyens of Berlin dub techno. The album begins with “Gaseous,” a birdsong field recording looped and rolled out over chorused dub pads, Monolake’s Hongkong emptied of people and half-returned to the jungle. Appleblim reflects on his love of birdsong, mentioning in a label Q&A how slowing down bird calls draws out their natural glissandos and sonic density that usually lie beyond the limits of human perception—certainly a ‘quiet detail’ if there ever was one. “Warmth” slings out a spindly but still implacably British breakbeat, something that can also be dredged warm and flickering from the depths of “Globule.” The two most percussive tracks, “Crow Crag” and “Weather Vane,” arrive next Both are driving but in the style of tape hiss-drenched somnambulant fugues rather than being dancefloor ready. The tracks represent dub techno annealed with dubsteppy low-end density and melodic experimentation; the former track layers in bits of Tangerine Dream-esque arpeggiation while chimes punctuate the latter like hypnic jerks. “Seagull” closes the set, the closest thing to a conventional ambient track built almost entirely from a swirling foghorn sample laced with seagull cries. This return to the water and air binds together the cycle of life, of which Liminal Tides’ antimonies are only a part of a coherent whole. (Marcello Ursic)

items.body: That Porous Line follows as a deliberate shift—letting in just enough light to see differently without abandoning the dark corners they prefer to inhabit. Push For Night arrives here as a natural fit That Porous Line by Push For Night   Room40 has been one of experimental music’s most important and quietly consistent labels since Lawrence English founded it in Brisbane in 2000. Over 25 years and more than 300 releases, it has built a catalog that spans electroacoustic composition, musique concrète, ambient, and avant-garde sound art—releasing work from Ben Frost, Tujiko Noriko, William Basinski, Grouper, and dozens of others. English works from a home studio built beneath a storage room containing literally a ton of records, an apt metaphor for a label that operates under the weight of its own history while continuing to push forward. Push For Night arrives here as a natural fit.​ The duo of Oliver Chapoy—Brooklyn-based musician, producer, and engineer known for his work with Saxon Shore, Warm Ghost, and collaborations with Helado Negro and Mikael Jorgensen of Wilco and James Elliott, Louisville, KY-based and equally steeped in experimental and post-rock sensibility, began their collaboration in 2017 and have been slowly building a body of work that lives at the intersection of electroacoustic processing, collage, and abstract sound construction. Their previous Room40 release Lapsed Gasps was a dense, intense record built around Jon Mueller‘s archived percussion recordings, processed through heavy electronics. That Porous Line follows as a deliberate shift—letting in just enough light to see differently without abandoning the dark corners they prefer to inhabit. “It’s Sure To Be Dark If You Shut Your Eyes” is a standout. The drums and glitched phaser of what sounds like a rolling percussion or hit every 8 to 16 bars is beautiful to the ear. There is a lot of stereo panning at play with their sound elements throughout, and while there really isn’t any persistent melody taking place, this leans more toward sound play and effects stacking—how many effects can they layer onto the same overlying loop until it gets absolutely destroyed and becomes something else. That question is the compositional engine driving a lot of this album, and here it’s applied with precision rather than aggression. “Idler’s Reward” is another strong one as far as melodic content goes—its emotional build and three-part structure make it a compelling standpoint for emotional construction. The song has three distinct sections if you hear it that way. What sounds like a marking drum echoing in the background is ringed with delay and echo on particular instruments and synths, making it interesting to listen to as it unfolds. Right at the six-minute mark, a highpass filter is applied to a looping note being echoed as a beautiful clarinet, played by Zachary Koeber—emerges as the second section of the track, playing out until 7:39 where the third section arrives with no warning: distorted, filtered guitar chords coming in and echoing to their own death. It is a fascinating build piece that earns every minute of its eight-plus-minute runtime. “Bait Is Lowered” continues the album’s definition of itself as a collection of building emotional pieces. Another fascinating piece of sounds. The incredible thing about experimental ambience like this is how long you can keep the listener engaged with the sounds being created and fatiguing them with noise or drone. Halfway through this track there’s a disruption—what can only be described as if you took a drum beat and submerged it in a bucket of water and started washing it aggressively as it builds up with suds. The music is very much imaginative. “Turned Slowly And Slowly Turned” is another dark piece with very subtle coos and creaky electronic rolls simulating what sounds like electronic animals or chirps, separated into two distinctive zones, far away and reverbed out on one side, the subtle coos chirping consistently back and forth softly on the other, no effects on them but slowed. Distortion play at its finest. “Push For Night describes their process as decorating the cave and inviting specters to reveal a message, trying to catch something in the semi-dark.” ~J. Batista “That Porous Line” is actually a beautiful closer, not the one expected after listening to this piece, but one that sounds genuinely immersive. The concept and theme of the album is still present, the bizarre distortions remain, but the melodies are toned down. Towards the end of the track there may be recycled field recordings surfacing, not to the naked ear but the trained one would catch it. The overall listen is actually pleasing, which for Push For Night is itself a notable statement. This is fundamentally an effects album and it shows, in the best possible way. The structure of experimentation with guitars and ambience has come a long way from the post-rock tradition that both Chapoy and Elliott carry in their backgrounds, and what That Porous Line represents is those backgrounds fully dissolved into something that no longer resembles where it came from. Push For Night describes their process as decorating the cave and inviting specters to reveal a message, trying to catch something in the semi-dark. On That Porous Line, they caught more than they usually let go of, and the result is their most emotionally varied and accessible work yet, which for this duo still means strange, flickering, and lit by crepuscular light. That’s the appeal. That Porous Line is available on Room40. [Bandcamp] That Porous Line by Push For NightThe post Push For Night :: That Porous Line (Room40) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: “MASKARA / مسكرة” had been teased for months before Saint Levant released it as the lead single from his third studio album, AFANDI / افندي, a 12-track record pulling from the era of Arab pop icons such as George Wassouf and Kadim Al Saher. On the track, Saint Levant is joined by Mohammed Assaf, who built his name on his defining anthem “Ana Dammi Falastini,” which turned him into one of the most recognised voices in the region after he won Arab Idol in 2013. Assaf’s roots are tied directly to the 1948 Nakba: his mother’s family was displaced from Bayt Daras and his father’s from Beersheba. Born in Misrata, Libya, he grew up in Gaza after his family relocated there Saint Levant, born in Jerusalem, carries his own parallel history of displacement into the collaboration, most directly heard on “Deira,” a song named for his father’s hotel on the Gaza seafront that was destroyed in an Israeli airstrike. Built around straightforward Arabic pop, “Maskara” itself is a celebration of Palestine and the shared cultural heritage of both artists. It perfectly introduces AFANDI, an album Saint Levant calls an ongoing dialogue between past and present—designed to bring listeners back to the region’s musical golden age. You can stream, listen to and purchase your copy of AFANDI / افندي  HERE The post Daily Discovery: Saint Levant, Mohammed Assaf – MASKARA / مسكرة appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — I'm a sucker for flashy weird cover art which in this case features some sort of giraffe-necked girlin the company of cyan backed stripes and bubble curlers. Add some wily angularity of classicUnivers Zero or Present based avant-prog and my interest is peaked. The Seattle based TROOT emergedfrom the band's namesake Tim Root who assembled a fiery chamber prog band that consists of 10musicians and takes a journey through the crossroads of classic chamber prog, avant-jazz and freeimprovisation. The band released its so far one off CONSTANCE AND THE WAITING in 2018 with anensemble that was handpicked from some of the most demanding and obscure underground acts in theranks of the experimental music universe.Root is the head honcho here and began his career as a classically trained pianist therefore thepresence of his piano-based charm is a dominant force throughout this album's six tracks with a 411/2 minute run. With 10 players on board this is the wonderful world of controlled chaos with theusual rock instrumentation of two guitarists, two bassists and a drummer along with the skronkyeffects of a saxophone and the expected chamber part of the equation in this case delivers by meansof the violin however there are ample offerings of an accordion adding some Mediterranean cafeelegance to the mix. While the star of the show is Root and his keyboard charming antics, the restof the band is quite competent delivering raucous avant-prog uprooting with the first two tracks"Axe For The Frozen Sea Within" and "Dance Elena" running the gamut of time signature frenzies atbreakneck speed to eerie atmospheric breakouts.While the album starts off on a high note, Root unfortunately steers things into a more pianorecital type of number on "Palasidai" which slows down the tempo and feisty knotty workouts severalnotches and rather serves as a breather that bucks the trend of atonal dissonance in favor of a moreballady even melodic piece that sounds a bit out of place although not bad per se. "Venice Of TheSky" jumps back into the avant-prog mind [%*!#]ery with stronger doses of jazz added to the mix andthe missing energy oomf that was missing from the previous track. And then another rather sleepyballad type of piano-based track with "Hollow By Footsteps" which sounds more like a 1950s jazzballad than anything that belongs on this album and IMHO the weakest track of the lot even if notbad if included under a different album mood setting. The album is redeemed by the knotty closer"Joey" which reverts back to the UZ meets Art Zoyd on steroids playbook and generates a scorcher ofan ending.Overall not a bad album save the two tracks that derail the momentum. Despite the furor of nastyavant-prog crafted on this album, the band unfortunately sounds a bit too close to its influencestherefore not really standing out as something unique and innovative although the band's excellentmusicianship makes this a very compelling listen nonetheless. It's not a perfect album due to thetwo lesser tracks that water down the whole album effect but even those tracks are not offensivelyawful in any way, just not suitable for what would make a cohesive album experience for me. Whilenot anything new under the sun at this point, the musical outfit known as TROOT nevertheless derivesan above competence level of crafty Rock In Opposition styled avant-prog that navigates an all-instrumental trajectory at least until the frenetic and unexpected screaming at the end of "Joey"which adds a nice twist to the tale. I do very much this band returns with a more adventurous albumbut despite the flaws this is still a very pleasant nerd out for those of us who love thisadventurous prog exhibitions of grandeur.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Well, this album certainly pertains to the title, finding beauty and truth in musical form is a luxury that progressive rock can easily provide. Back in 2020 when leader Dave Bandana began this project, he immediately connected with some exemplary musicians, names like Peter Jones (surely one of the great British prog talents), American drummer Tim Gehrt, Welsh guitarist Gareth Cole and the illustrious Cosmograf Robin Armstrong (who left after the second album). The four mentioned though are still the core, firmly entrenched in heir own little universe, crowning their relationship with this splendid effort, as well as being their finest. Toss in wordsmith Brad Birzer, and the sterling lyrics come alive with profound poignancy. Nice expansive track to launch the listening experience, "Islands" has all the classic ingredients to make one lose themselves in an atoll of sonic pleasure. A heady combination of various stylistics seamlessly concocted to create escapism at its finest. Orchestral, Celtic, jazz, rock and folk tendencies unite as a common front, without any kind of tedium or overt simplicity. Initially silky smooth and ambient, the drama takes little time to divulge its many enjoyments, Gehrt's primal beat bashing along like a giant wave, Cole's tingling guitar behaving like a rudder, all captained along by Mr. Jones' exceptional storytelling voice. Like a sudden monsoon surging across the horizon, the latter's saxophone skills inject a sunny luminescence that can only make the heart race a tad faster. When the 'timeless' brass and axe decide to interweave, well, it is called magic for a reason! There goes my jaw again, fluttering away in the wind! I mean , WOW! Only a breezy pseudo-instrumental can express the willowing beauty of "Fallen Leaves", the numerous choral voices acting like foliage swept by Newton's discovery. Its brief yet arching voluptuousness and fragile pastoral sense evokes images of acceptance and serenity. An ideal set-up for the colossal wallop of "Arribabok", the suave Bandana bass underwrites the complete array of sophisticated sounds emanating from each instrument, proposing an almost funky vibe, yet Cole does experiment with Manzanera-like slivers from his insistent guitar and Jones does an extended Andy Mackay move on the saxophone. One can even detect a Paul Thompson sense on the drum kit. Proggy Roxy (my highest possible compliment)! Much like my very best friend Lazland, my favourite month is also October, being hopeless romantic Autumn fans me thinks, and on "October Sun", it's purely heartwarming in its utter innocence, verging on panacea for the soul of fall worshippers, 'until the sun shines through'. A hint of my all-time favourite album (Hero and Heroine by the Strawbs), what with choral mentions of shining and suns, the clanging Cole guitars even recollect fond memories of Dave Lambert. Thankfully, the Jones saxophone slams this into another jurisdiction as the jovial bass bops like a Mexican jumping bean (remember those?). My feet, my hands and my head were forcefully keeping the beat?.Fun times coming up soon . Speaking of which, "From Empty Trees" has a monstrous and trebly bass running rampant on this instrumental, the ebullient synthesizers slipping between the branches, organ unafraid to pomp as well as supply ceremony and finish of the proceedings with a scorching guitar solo just to keep the forest ranger faraway from Yogi Bear (let us not forget Bubu). Epic time to rejoice once again, "A View" offers an orchestral and rhythmic foundation for Jones to emote vocally like only he can. His ability to plead, to beg, to steal and to borrow in his various inflections is absolutely masterful. Every single vowel and consonant are clear as the water in that lagoon on that island, where this stellar journey began. Talk about escapism, I have been somewhere else since the very first note, very track a joyful paradise. "Harder to See" is next and it's hard to imagine that the overt atmosphere keeps glowing like a spiritual fireball , 'I sit and wonder! You have a plan and you can', believe you me! An inquisitive sentiment on the complexity of confusion, of misdirection, of illusion, call what you want, its only words. The lamenting backing harmony vocals showcase the despair. Being a prog archivist and having a ramrod strong memory of all my hundreds of concerts , "Rewind" seems to wander back to gentler times, as befits us old geezers who still feel comfort in a youth very well lived. There is quite the classic golden age of 70s Prog feel to this finale , a carefree time when labels were meaningless and overt criticisms wiped away by astonished eyes and ears, every occasion we walked into a record store or a concert hall. Even the smells remain vivid to this day. The empowering orchestral send-off with acoustic guitars, flutes and mellotrons in tow is plain orgasmic. Rael must be on a poster somewhere in the studio, its eerie and yet so utterly expressive. Perhaps it was due to the Fly on the Windshield. 5 faultless things definitely worth remembering (who, what, where, when and why)

The music rocks, swings, has soulful passages and is somewhat catchy all at the same time. The lineup for "Quube" is - Chad Wackerman (drums), Alex Machacek (guitar), Jimmy Haslip (bass), and Steve Hunt (keys). Every song is engaging and if you know these players, there is no surprise that the musicianship is out of this world. If you're familiar with Chad's previous solo albums there is a high probability you will love this. So far this is only available digitally, but it sounds amazing thanks to Steve Hunt and the group. Highly recommend to fusion fans.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Despite the fact that this is a reunion album in which the band performs cover versions of it's old material, it's always nice to hear Quidam music--and to hear them reunited with former founding lead singer Emilia Nazaruk (n�e Derkowska) is a real treat--even these 30 years later. The other founding members present from that wonderful first album from 1996 are guitarist Maciej Meller and keyboard maestro Zbigniew Florek--the two dudes who have been writing the bulk of the band's music since day one. My favorite song straight away is the gorgeous "Jesteś (w labiryncie myśli) / You Are (in the Labyrinth of Thoughts)"--a song in which Emilia proves how she's still got all the skills and talents that she put on display back in 1996. "One Day We Find" also avails itself with great power as Bartosz Kossowicz earns his place among the pantheon of great Polish prog vocalists.The album's best song, however, may be its beautiful finale: "Spotykanie" (7:32) Here we have a remake of a song that first appeared on the band's last previous album, 2012's Saiko. I always love it when Quidam (or any band from non-English speaking countries) sings in their native tongue. Here Bartosz and Emilia take turns and even back one another as well as dueting within a gorgeous soundscape of guitars, synth washes, piano chords, and lilting flute melodies over Mariusz and Maciej Wr�blewski's warm and comforting bed of hypnotic rhythms. Then there's Maciej Meller's wonderful soaring guitar solo in the sixth and seventh minutes before Bartosz, Emilia, and Zbigniew so delicately tuck us in (for a wonderful night of peaceful sleep). Bravissimo! Great ending song to a fine comeback album! (14.125/15)Bass player Mariusz Zi�łkowski continues doing his great job of filling the shoes of the band's previous bassists as does flutist Jacek Zasada filling an equally-important role to this band's traditional sound. It's so nice to have Quidam back and still going strong!

items.body: Review by XixoTheRock — After dissapearing for some time of social media, Cherc�n has suddenly come back with a single!Which our first sneak peek to their next album, which they have confirmed (via Instagram) that theyare working on.Cherc�n has gone acid rock, and I am enjoying it, a lot if I'm to be honest. The single still hasband's DNA embedded in it, which means it still has a heavy, energetic and vanguardist approachto music, luckily enough, they were able to balance that with good production, something which Icomplained about on my review to their previous LP. Something I'd like to point out is how thissingle is a little more mellow for a hard rock/acid rock track, do I complain? No, that is becausethe music is astounding and hypnotic, and more mature stylistically than their previous work.Something I do not accustom to analyze in my reviews is the cover art, If I'm not mistaken, the lasttime I did so was with "The bedlam on Goliath" by The Mars Volta (which coincidentally, seems to bea big influence for the band, specially Pe�a's vocal delivery). This cover art is an edited pictureof the surface of mars, taken by NASA during their reconnaissance missions during the 70's, it hascirculated the internet and sporadically gotten famous every few years. This picture is without adoubt, fitting for the concept of the track, which orbits around the concept of pareidolia, apsychological phenomenon which consists of the brain triggering pattern recognition and observing(usually) human faces where they are not present. Despite being fitting for the lyrics/concept, I amnot in for taking pre-existing pictures/plastic art works for sleeve art, I consider this practiceto be exhibiting of low initiative, therefore I am not excited about the cover art. Does this takepoints away from the single? Sort of, since cover art does not really impact the composition of thetrack, then I can look over this, but for prog rock, a genre known for it multimedia and grandioseapproach to art, it feels incredibly dissapoiting.Music wise, I consider this single to depart from Cherc�n's previous vanguardist, metal and fusionapproach, taking one which is much closer to acid rock and heavy prog. The track starts with a cleanmath rock guitar riff, the delay and compression being reminiscent of Rush's songs like "RedBarchetta" or "Different strings", being accompanied by a simple bass line, and after Pe�a's vocalsstart, we get our transition to our Hendrix and Rodr�guez L�pez's heavy riffs. The track has somesynthesizer riffs which are played with grace and intricate metrics, which are the the backbone ofthe psychedelic textures, they are slimy spots on our vision which make us feel like we're spinningaround. There are two transposed and dueling saxophones which are the texture that grounds us alittle from our trance to space, the mixture of Synths and Saxophone polymetrics/polyrhythms createa psychedelic eter which makes us feel like we are floating in a dimension of patterns and figureswhich are celestial, supernatural, powerful and colourful. The jarring, clean then heavy then cleanagain guitar riffs are what give the track it's heavy acid rock feel, they are frenetic, much moresimple than Cherc�n's debut album riffs but still quite interesting, specially tonally, they arereminiscent of Tool and The grateful dead in a lot of ways, one of which is it's repetitive butheavy patterns, despite being in 4/4 most of the time, the bass also acts much more like a secondguitar instead of a rhythmic instrument, much like Metallica's original bassit Cliff Burton'sapproach to his instrument. It is the mixture of psychedelic textures with heavier riffs and amoderately energetic drumming which separate this from Avant Garde Fusion metal and drives thesingle towards Acid rock, it is heavy, psychedelic, but yet balanced and soft. The feel o get islike I am swimming in a sea looming over the mysterious auroras of Saturn and it's moons, it'scaptivating and dreamlike, but the energy is what makes this track NOT be a boring mellow space rocktrack, which is what it could have become, controlled frenzy and moderate energy that doesn't reachaggressiveness is what makes this track unique, very much like what Jimi Hendrix would write orplay.I think it'd be redundant to mention the incredible musicianship and dynamic of the musicians, sinceI have already written about this in the past (check my Cherc�n's LP debut review if you areinterested in the Chilean scene!), so I will elaborate further on what improved frok their previousrecord, mistakes they patched. I'd start with the most important thing which is Pe�a's vocals, whichhad been buried previously under layers and layers of loud instrumentation and a very mumble likedelivery, Pe�a finally articulates his vocals much more and this makes it much easier and lessdraining to try to appreciate the lyrics and their relation to the instrumentation, while alsokeeping his energy that accompanies the instrumentation perfectly, his influences by Cedric BixleyZavala have paid off! The production has also improved significantly when compared to their previousrecord, it's much more clear and balanced, less reverberating and recorded with better equipment,this I theorize is due to the new financing and help from organizations such as the Chileangovernment via their ministry of culture. The musicians are already well trained, experimented andvirtuoso so not much more to say regarding this. Does the single have flaws their previous recorddid? I'd say Peña still doesn't articulate to it's fullest yet, despite it all, the single denotes asignificant improvement compared to their previous work.The lyrics certainly are interesting! They are spiritual, very spiritual if I have to be honest,focussing on transcendence from the mundane human body and reaching it's fullest potential, thisexplored through the lens of our relationship to the material world around us. Those who arefamilliarezed with German idealism and Descartes's thought will recognize the resemblances theselyrics have to key concepts of the record, such as the thesis and antithesis Hegel speaks about, orhow Immanuel Kant critiqued pure reason and the idealists thought of how we can't actually accessthe world around us if it's not through perception and subjectivity. This is while the single iscalled "Pareidolia" and why it leaves heavy vanguardism behind for an acid rock approach. I amparticularly fond of the closing line "Elijo el infinito" (I choose infinity), which sums andsynthetices the entire track astonishingly great.Overall, I'd consider this single to be a great example of how to write acid rock in the 21st Centuryand it certainly does promise us a great record from Cherc�n in the near future, leaving an openquestion before us, will Cherc�n be able to top the biggest Chilean prog and art rock bands of thescene with their next record? Only time will tell!

items.body: Review by alainPP — Andrew Latimer, guitarist of the legendary band Camel, releases his second album?a continuous, seamless suite that eschews strict timing in favor of serenity, atmosphere, contemplation, and memories."From The Vault" is a suite Andrew created to help him move past his health issues?drawing on more than just his archives. "Those Times" opens with an Eastern flair before shifting to a deep riff and Gilmour-esque prog vocals. It evokes memories of his last tour?hence the cinematic sound effects?and features an Indian-inspired detour with flute, djembe, monolithic keyboards, and strings; "Why did you Lie?" is the question posed. The guitar solo is spellbinding, with a neo-classical keyboard style from Pete reminiscent of Manfred Mann. "Isolation" offers a Western vibe akin to Knopfler, Rea, or even Chet Atkins?a Southern-style track that flows endlessly. "Heaven," co-written by Pete, stays true to the Camel sound with divine flute work; it is a love song whose freshness brings to mind the Electric Light Orchestra."Clock Upon the Wall" emerges with folk banjo and conventional pop instrumentation, alongside a distinct bluesy feel. "Railroad Tracks" features metronomic drumming, a gentle start, and Alan Parsons-esque keyboards?a lovely memory?though the vocal duet and repetitive, soft-pop sound become somewhat grating. "Dingley Dell" uses piano to capture the eccentricities of the hero from Dickens' *The Pickwick Papers*, while a Genesis-like air rises from the label's signature charismatic atmosphere. "Clouds" concludes with an instrumental section where the guitar shines, surrendering to ethereal keyboards?a solemn moment reminiscent of one of Queen's final tracks.Andrew Latimer releases this musical suite. Orchestral arrangements provide the symphonic touch needed to elevate tracks that otherwise feel more like demos or outtakes.

items.body: Two years ago I reviewed the first release in this series, a Mahler Ninth (Alpha, 2024 – review), arguing that many of Philipp von Steinaecker’s contentions for “period performance” Mahler were unconvincing. There is no need to rehash those points here. In the liner notes for this release, Steinaecker describes the scholarly work done to ensure that the Mahler Academy Orchestra’s playing (vibrato, bowings, articulation, portamento, and the instruments themselves) matches what Mahler worked with at the time of composition. Symphony No. 5 Amazon Presto Apple But the conceit that the instruments and playing techniques of Mahler’s time result in a more accurate and successful performance is wrong-headed. Ultimately, the point of any recording is its worthiness for repeated listening. The playing here is good, and we hear the scholarship in action throughout. I find this performance more convincing than the team’s Ninth, but as a Mahler Fifth it does not match, let alone eclipse, the performances from Tilson Thomas in San Francisco, Tennstedt in London, Chailly in Amsterdam, Abbado in Berlin, and Bernstein in Vienna, to list just a few. The scholarship is on display right after the opening movement’s trumpet fanfare: the strings play the first theme (track 1, 1’10”) with minimal vibrato, heightened articulation, shorter bow strokes, and added portamento. But it comes across as a lecture demonstration rather than a musical performance. Where is the numbed grief heard in the Bernstein and Tennstedt readings? Both conductors use articulation, vibrato, and a little portamento to conjure that grief, more successfully than Steinaecker does here. He keeps tight control throughout the faster middle section (5’35”), never letting the music feel as if it might go off the rails. Yet we have a piano roll of Mahler playing a transcription of this music in which he creates a wildness suggesting derailment is imminent. The composer wanted emotional extremes. Should that not be the goal of every conductor of this music? The second movement takes off at a fast tempo but again lacks that last ounce of wildness. The playing is impressive, but I doubt any composer would choose technical perfection over emotional expression. As the fury subsides, Steinaecker chooses a dramatically slower tempo that loses momentum, and too little is made of the cellos’ lament a few minutes later. After the chorale climax, the opening music returns, finally as unhinged as it should have been at the start of the movement. The Scherzo brings two interpretive issues into focus. Steinaecker sets significant contrasts of tempo, surely intended for a more impassioned reading, but all too often the slower tempos bring a loss of energy and momentum. Bernstein and Tennstedt adopt tempos just as slow, if not slower, yet the tension never slackens as it does here. There is plenty of character when the orchestra is not focused on scholarly point-making, but just as often the playing seems intent on demonstrating “authentic” differences at the expense of the music’s emotional arc. Philipp von Steinaecker. The Adagietto, chaste and sweetly sung, frustrates: in a reading intent on honoring what Mahler intended, the speed is too slow. Two Mahler disciples with distinctly different interpretive styles recorded this movement within three decades of the composer’s death. Willem Mengelberg’s 1926 reading takes roughly seven minutes, and Bruno Walter’s 1938 reading roughly eight. Both had heard Mahler conduct this music, and in a performance predicated on honoring Mahler’s intentions, surely Steinaecker (9’05”) should be faster, which would arguably suit his orchestra’s less resonant gut strings. In a reading so focused on point-making, this tempo feels willfully out of place. In the Rondo-Finale Steinaecker finally loosens the reins, and the orchestra clearly revels in playing this music at a driven tempo. At last I sense the energy and power missing from the earlier movements. Steinaecker’s Coda is perhaps the most compelling and distinctive aspect of his interpretation; it would certainly bring any audience to its feet. If only the same freedom and imagination had been applied to the earlier movements. While I found more to appreciate here than in the team’s earlier Ninth, I remain unconvinced of any greater authenticity, and cannot recommend this performance ahead of those mentioned above. Recommended Comparisons Mahler: Symphony No. 5 Bernstein | Tennstedt | Chailly | Abbado | Tilson Thomas The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult released its fourth studio album, “13 Above the Night”, on 7 September 1993 through Interscope Records. The album turns 33 this year. Buzz McCoy produced and wrote the album, recording at Ground Control Studios in Los Angeles with Fred Giannelli co-producing and Eric Stitt Greedy and Jay Lean engineering. “13 Above the Night” was the band’s first release for Interscope and its first album recorded with touring members Levi Levi on bass, Otto Matrix on drums, Trash Kavity on guitar, and Chicago house vocalist Shawn Christopher. Lydia Lunch co-wrote and sang on “Dirty Little Secrets”. Guitarists Bruce Manning and Luc van Acker also contributed. What is on ’13 Above the Night’ The original 13-track edition runs “The Velvet Edge”, “Delicate Terror”, “Badlife”, “Dirty Little Secrets”, “China De Sade”, “Dimentia 66”, “Final Blindness”, “Blue Buddha”, “Starmartyr”, “Electrical Soul Wish”, “13 Above the Night”, “Disko Fleshpot” and “Savage Sexteen”. A 1999 Rykodisc reissue added two remixes, “Blue Buddha (Master of the UltraFlesh Mix)” and “Electrical Soul Wish (Miss Hate Mix)”, as bonus tracks. The album samples dialogue from two films: “Disko Fleshpot” lifts spoken lines from the 1969 film “Midnight Cowboy”, and “Starmartyr” samples the 1976 horror film “Squirm”. The band toured the US from October to December 1993 in support of the album, with Machines of Loving Grace as the opening act. About My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult formed in Chicago in 1987 around Groovie Mann (Frankie Nardiello) and Buzz McCoy (Marston Daley), building an industrial dance sound around samples, disco rhythm sections and B-movie and exploitation-film imagery. The band released its debut album, “I See Good Spirits and I See Bad Spirits”, in 1988 through Wax Trax! Records, followed by “Confessions of a Knife” in 1990 and “Sexplosion!” in 1991, before moving to Interscope for “13 Above the Night” in 1993. “Hit & Run Holiday” followed in 1995, continuing the band’s run of major-label albums before further releases across the 2000s and 2010s. My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult has remained active on tour into the 2020s, including a fall 2025 run reported in My Life With The Thrill Kill Kult announces fall tour ‘Delicate Terror: Part 1’, taking its name from a track on “13 Above the Night”, and a spring 2026 US run covered in Heavy Halo join My Life With the Thrill Kill Kult for spring 2026 U.S. dates.

items.body: Lacrimosa released its eleventh studio album, “Revolution”, on 7 September 2012 through Hall of Sermon (catalogue reference HOS 8030). The album turns 14 this year. Tilo Wolff produced the record himself. Spotify’s release metadata lists the album a day earlier, on 6 September 2012; Wikipedia and Discogs both confirm 7 September as the official release date. Wolff sang and played piano, bass and drum programming across the record, with Anne Nurmi on keyboards and additional vocals. Two guest musicians joined the sessions: guitarist Mille Petrozza of Kreator and drummer Stefan Schwarzmann of Accept, alongside guitarists J.P. Genkel and Henrik Flyman, drummers Arturo Garcia and Manne Uhlig, violinist Christina Grabka, and the orchestra Die Spielmann-Schnyder. What is on Lacrimosa’s ‘Revolution’ The album runs 10 tracks: “Irgendein Arsch ist immer unterwegs”, “If the World Stood Still a Day”, “Verloren”, “This Is the Night”, “Interlude – Feuerzug (Part 1)”, “Feuerzug (Part 2)”, “Refugium”, “Weil Du Hilfe brauchst”, “Rote Sinfonie” and the title track “Revolution”. The cover art depicts the band’s recurring harlequin mascot standing over debris, waving a flag. German magazine Orkus named “Revolution” its album of the month for October 2012, and Powermetal.de highlighted Petrozza’s guitar work while noting the album’s more direct songwriting compared to earlier Lacrimosa records. The album peaked at number 35 on the German album charts. About Lacrimosa Lacrimosa began in 1990 when Tilo Wolff recorded the demo tape “Clamor” in Germany, releasing the debut album “Angst” in 1991 through his own label, Hall of Sermon, which he founded the same year. Finnish musician Anne Nurmi joined in 1993, becoming Wolff’s permanent creative partner. The band’s early studio run continued through “Einsamkeit” (1992), “Satura” (1993), “Inferno” (1995), “Stille” (1997), “Elodia” (1999), “Fassade” (2001) and “Echos” (2003), moving from Wolff’s gothic rock beginnings toward the fuller orchestral and metal-oriented sound that later defined “Sehnsucht” (2009) and “Revolution” (2012). “Hoffnung” followed “Revolution” in 2015. After a run of years without new studio material, Lacrimosa confirmed a new album was in production, reported in Worldwide paper shortage delays release new Lacrimosa album and The legendary Lacrimosa is coming back with a new studio album, and it will be released this year after all!. That album, “Lament”, was announced in January 2025, covered in Lacrimosa returns with an all new album: ‘Lament’. The band also released the double live album “Nachts” through Hall of Sermon, covered in Introducing ‘Nachts’: Lacrimosa Double Live CD on Hall of Sermon.

items.body: Gary Numan, the English synth-pop and new wave musician who had spent the previous two years fronting Tubeway Army, released his debut solo album “The Pleasure Principle” on 7 September 1979 through Beggars Banquet. The album turns 47 this year. Numan produced it himself at Marcus Recording Studios in London, with Harvey Webb and Rikki Sylvan engineering and mixing, and Julian Mills and Melvyn Abrahams mastering at Strawberry Mastering. The record arrived about six months after “Replicas”, his second and final album with Tubeway Army, and reached number 1 on the UK Albums Chart. How Gary Numan built ‘The Pleasure Principle’ without a guitar Numan dropped electric guitar from the sessions entirely. In its place he layered the Minimoog he had already used on “Replicas” with a Polymoog, leaning on that keyboard’s Vox Humana preset, an ARP Odyssey, and a Synare 3 for synthetic percussion. Flanging, phasing and reverb ran across the mixes, and solo viola and violin parts sat inside otherwise electronic arrangements. Paul Gardiner played bass, Chris Payne handled keyboards and viola, and Cedric Sharpley played drums and percussion. Billy Currie of Ultravox added fadeout violin to “Tracks” and “Conversation”, and Garry Robson sang backing vocals on “Conversation”. Side one of the original UK LP ran “Airlane”, “Metal”, “Complex”, “Films” and “M.E.”; side two ran “Tracks”, “Observer”, “Conversation”, “Cars” and “Engineers”. The sleeve took its title and its staging from René Magritte’s painting “The Pleasure Principle”, with Numan seated in the pose of the original but surrounded by artificial objects, including a glowing purple Perspex pyramid where Magritte had placed a stone. Tony Escott illustrated the cover, Geoff Howes shot the photography, and Malti Kidia art directed. First UK copies came with a printed inner sleeve carrying the lyrics on one side and a band picture on the other. “Cars” appeared as a single in August 1979, ahead of the album, and reached number 9 in the United States and number 1 in Canada. “Complex” followed that November and peaked at number 6 in the UK across a nine-week chart run. Numan later said he regretted the choice and that “Metal” should have gone out instead. Reviews at the time were mixed. Robert Christgau of The Village Voice described the album as “Metal Machine Music goes easy-listening”. Red Starr, writing in Smash Hits, called it “not bad, mind you”, but “much too similar” to “Replicas”. Record Mirror’s Simon Ludgate wrote that “detachment and distance are painstakingly sewn into every track”. Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark supported the UK leg of the tour that followed, a production built around banks of neon lights and two radio-controlled pyramids that moved across the stage. Beggars Banquet issued a 30th anniversary edition on 21 September 2009 with a second disc of demos, outtakes and live recordings, and a 40th anniversary set, “The Pleasure Principle: The First Recordings”, on 11 October 2019 across double coloured vinyl and 2CD. The album’s material has kept circulating outside Numan’s own catalogue. Nine Inch Nails covered “Metal” on “Things Falling Apart” in 2000, Afrika Bambaataa recorded it in 2004, and Basement Jaxx built “Where’s Your Head At” on “M.E.”. Side-Line covered a more recent reading of the same track in [melter] covers Gary Numan hit ‘Metal’ – Watch the video now, and the wider tribute traffic in Gary Numan revisited by various dark wave bands for a vinyl release – check the first video. About Gary Numan Gary Numan was born Gary Anthony James Webb in Hammersmith, London, in 1958. He formed Tubeway Army in 1977 as a punk band with his uncle Jess Lidyard on drums and Paul Gardiner on bass, and switched to synthesizers after finding a Minimoog left in a studio during the sessions for the group’s self-titled debut, released in 1978. The band’s second album, “Replicas”, came out in 1979 and reached number 1 in the UK, carried by the single “Are ‘Friends’ Electric?”, which also topped the UK chart. Numan dropped the group name that year, keeping Gardiner in the band and adding Chris Payne on keyboards and Cedric Sharpley on drums. “The Pleasure Principle” followed on 7 September 1979 and gave Numan a second UK number 1 album in the same year. “Telekon” arrived in September 1980 and did the same. He then moved through a long run of albums on his own Numa label and elsewhere, including “Warriors” in 1983, before his commercial standing in Britain fell away through the second half of the decade. The catalogue kept its influence regardless, and by the late 1990s a younger generation of industrial and electronic acts had begun citing and covering it openly. Numan’s later work brought him back to the same audience Side-Line reports on. “Splinter (Songs From A Broken Mind)” was announced in 2013, covered here in Gary Numan announces new ‘Splinter (Songs From A Broken Mind)’ album and tour – listen to first track!, and “Savage (Songs from a Broken World)” followed in 2017, reported in Gary Numan to release new ‘Savage (Songs from a Broken World)’ album on double vinyl (with 2 bonus tracks). He talked through his studio methods in Gary Numan – ‘After doing this for over 35 years I still get excited about what’s around the corner’ – Tech-Talk with DJ Wildhoney. Collaborations have run alongside the solo records. He worked with John Foxx on the release covered in John Foxx and Gary Numan collaborate on ’21st Century: a Man, a Woman and a City’ album – out in 2 physical versions, joined Jean-Michel Jarre’s “Electronica” project alongside Pet Shop Boys, appeared on a Chris Liebing album in 2018, and toured North America in 2023 in direct support of Ministry, as reported in Ministry announces 2023 headline tour dates with direct support from Gary Numan & Front Line Assembly. The Tubeway Army years were documented in the book covered in Gary Numan biography ‘Tubeway Daze: The Untold Story Of Tubeway Army’ hits the book shelves. Forty-seven years on, “The Pleasure Principle” remains the album Numan returned to most often on stage, performing it in full on dedicated tours in 2009 and again across the United States in 2010.

items.body: Siouxsie & The Banshees released their second studio album, “Join Hands”, on 7 September 1979 through Polydor Records. The album turns 47 this year. Nils Stevenson, the band’s manager, produced it with Mike Stavrou, recording at AIR Studios in London during May and June 1979. Ian Morais assisted with engineering. The album took the First World War as its lyrical starting point, after the band had watched televised scenes of repression in Iran and observed the two-minute silence marking the war dead in November 1978. The opening track, “Poppy Day”, set words from John McCrae’s poem “In Flanders Fields” against tolling bells; “Icon” and “Regal Zone” carried the theme further, the latter addressing the Iranian revolution. The closing track, a 14-minute studio recording of “The Lord’s Prayer”, reprised the song the band had famously performed at their debut show at the 100 Club Punk Festival in September 1976. What is on Siouxsie & The Banshees’ ‘Join Hands’ Side one ran “Poppy Day”, “Regal Zone”, “Placebo Effect”, “Icon” and “Premature Burial”, the last of which gave the album its title. Side two opened with “Playground Twist”, the sole single, followed by “Mother/Oh Mein Papa” and “The Lord’s Prayer”. Siouxsie Sioux sang and played piano, John McKay played guitar and saxophone, Steven Severin played bass, and Kenny Morris played drums and percussion. A 2006 remastered reissue added the non-album single “Love in a Void” and the previously unreleased instrumental “Infantry” as bonus tracks. Rob O’Connor designed the released sleeve, built around photography of four statues from London’s Guards Memorial, after Polydor rejected the band’s original artwork, a distorted Holy Communion card image designed by John Maybury. “Join Hands” reached number 13 on the UK Albums Chart and was later certified silver by the BPI. It was the last album to feature the band’s original lineup: McKay and Morris quit abruptly on the day of release, hours before a show at the Capitol Theatre in Aberdeen, and never returned. Siouxsie later described the record as reflecting the band’s state at the time: “We were lonely and isolated and that comes across in the music.” She added that “musically, Join Hands was an uncompromising album but it still sounds modern today.” Author Simon Reynolds has cited the album, alongside “Juju”, as a major source of gothic rock’s sound and lyrical themes. About Siouxsie & The Banshees Siouxsie & The Banshees formed in London in 1976, growing out of the Bromley Contingent scene around the Sex Pistols. The original lineup, with Siouxsie Sioux on vocals, Steven Severin on bass, and a rotating cast including Sid Vicious on drums for their debut performance, played “The Lord’s Prayer” as an improvised, 20-minute set at the 100 Club Punk Festival in September 1976. The band signed to Polydor Records in 1978 and released its debut album, “The Scream”, that November, followed by “Join Hands” in 1979. McKay and Morris’s departure on the day of “Join Hands”‘ release forced a rapid rebuild: Robert Smith of The Cure and briefly Budgie filled in on the resumed tour, and John McGeoch joined on guitar alongside Budgie on drums for “Kaleidoscope” in 1980, covered here in Siouxsie and the Banshees’ ‘Kaleidoscope’ turns 46 on 1 August. The band continued through “Juju” (1981), “A Kiss in the Dreamhouse” (1982), and the covers album “Through the Looking Glass” (1987), reaching a commercial peak with “Peepshow” (1988) and its hit single “Peek-a-Boo”, before “Superstition” (1991) and final album “The Rapture” (1995) closed the studio catalogue. The band disbanded in 1996; Siouxsie and Budgie continued as The Creatures. Siouxsie Sioux has remained active on Side-Line’s radar since, including a 2024 collaboration with Iggy Pop on “The Passenger” for a Magnum ad campaign, reported in Siouxsie Sioux and Iggy Pop collaborate on ‘The Passenger’ for Magnum Ice Cream ad – Out now, and former guitarist Jon Klein’s 2023 reworking of a Banshees classic with Jah Wobble, covered in Former Siouxsie & The Banshees guitarist Jon Klein teams up with Jah Wobble for a new version of a Siouxsie classic. Forty-seven years on, “Join Hands” remains the fault line between the band’s original punk-era lineup and the post-punk and gothic direction that followed.

items.body: Covenant released its ninth studio album, “Leaving Babylon”, on 6 September 2013 through Dependent Records in Europe (catalogue reference MINd 214/215). The album turns 13 this year. Metropolis Records issued it in the United States on 10 September 2013. Eskil Simonsson handled vocals and composition, with Daniel Jonasson on keys and vocoder, Andreas Catjar on keys and guitar, and Joakim Montelius contributing lyrics and patterns. Daniel Myer, who had left the band’s studio lineup after 2011’s “Modern Ruin” to focus on his own projects, still co-wrote the opening title track with Simonsson. “Leaving Babylon” was Andreas Catjar’s first album with Covenant. What is on Covenant’s ‘Leaving Babylon’ The album runs 10 tracks: “Leaving Babylon”, “Thy Kingdom Come”, “Last Dance”, “Prime Movers”, “I Walk Slow”, “For Our Time”, “Ignorance & Bliss”, “Auto (Circulation)”, “Not To Be Here” and “Leaving Babylon II”. The record was released across CD, a limited digipak CD edition, and vinyl in Europe, plus CD and digital editions through Metropolis in the US. About Covenant Covenant formed in Helsingborg, Sweden, in 1986, founded by Eskil Simonsson, Joakim Montelius and Clas Nachmanson. The band’s early EBM and future pop sound, shaped by acts including Front 242 and Kraftwerk, first reached record through the 1994 debut “Dreams of a Cryotank”, followed by “Sequencer” (1996) and “Europa” (1998). “United States of Mind” (2000) and “Northern Light” (2002) extended the band’s international reach, with “Northern Light” carrying the single “Bullet”. Daniel Myer joined for “Skyshaper” (2006) and “In Transit” (2007) before those studio duties eventually passed on. “Modern Ruin” followed in 2011, and “Leaving Babylon” arrived in 2013 as the first Covenant album with Andreas Catjar in the lineup. The band’s next studio album, “The Blinding Dark”, was released in 2016 through Dependent Records, covered here in Covenant – The Blinding Dark (CD Album – Dependent Records) and in the release interview Covenant: “The Blinding Dark” – release interview and tour updates. Andreas Catjar-Danielsson, who played keys and guitar on both “Leaving Babylon” and “The Blinding Dark”, died on 29 July 2024 after a long illness, reported in Andreas Catjar-Danielsson (Covenant) has lost battle against cancer. Covenant later issued the charity release “Andreas EP” through Dependent Records in his memory, covered in Covenant charity release ‘Andreas EP’ out now on Dependent Records.
